questions.prompt: A client times out and retries the same intended document analysis. Which identifier must stay stable?
questions.explanation: The operation ID represents one intended business effect and lets the server reconcile a retry with previously recorded state.

questions.prompt: The idempotency store finds the same operation ID with a different payload digest. What should happen?
options: Treat it as a normal retry
questions.explanation: One operation key cannot safely represent two intents; a conflict prevents accidental deduplication or overwrite of changed input.

questions.prompt: A database commit may have succeeded, but the worker lost the acknowledgement. What is the safest next action?
options: Reconcile authoritative state by operation ID
questions.explanation: An unknown outcome may already contain the effect, so the worker checks durable state before attempting another externally visible write.

questions.prompt: What does at-least-once queue delivery require from a mutating consumer?
questions.explanation: At-least-once delivery deliberately permits duplicates, so the application must make repeated logical operations safe.

questions.prompt: Document version 2 is committed before a delayed version 1 event arrives. What protects the projection?
questions.explanation: A conditional domain-version rule rejects stale events without relying on arrival order or unsynchronized worker clocks.

questions.prompt: Which failure should normally be terminal rather than retried?
questions.explanation: Authorization denial will not improve with time, and retrying it wastes capacity while obscuring a policy decision.

questions.prompt: A system receives 50 jobs/second and can sustainably complete 40. What happens under sustained load?
questions.explanation: Sustained arrival above service capacity accumulates unfinished work; retries can further amplify demand rather than create capacity.

questions.prompt: Which pair best exposes whether an asynchronous queue is failing its user-facing objective?
options: Oldest-message age and terminal completion latency
questions.explanation: Age and end-to-end terminal latency reveal how long accepted work waits and whether users receive outcomes on time.

questions.prompt: What is a dead-letter queue's operational role?
options: Quarantine with owned inspection and controlled redrive
questions.explanation: Dead-letter records require an owner, alert, diagnosis, repair, retention, and rate-limited idempotent redrive procedure.

questions.prompt: Which AWS pattern most directly fits independently processed work that must absorb bursts?
options: SQS work queue with bounded consumers
SNS alone as durable work ownership
questions.explanation: A work queue buffers bursty independent items and lets consumers scale within downstream concurrency and retry limits.

questions.prompt: A workflow service documents exactly-once execution. What remains unproven?
options: Every arbitrary downstream side effect occurs exactly once
questions.explanation: Workflow execution semantics do not create one atomic transaction across databases, emails, APIs, and other external effects.

questions.prompt: Why report delivery attempts per successful logical operation?
options: To measure work amplification and retry cost
questions.explanation: The ratio shows how much transport and dependency work each successful business outcome consumes, exposing retry storms.
